title: Weather and Climate
description: Weather is the day-to-day condition of the atmosphere. Temperature is measured with thermometers. Climate is the typical weather pattern of a region over a long time.

exercises.question: What is WEATHER?
choices: the long-term pattern of temperature for a region
the day-to-day conditions of the atmosphere (temperature, rain, wind)
exercises.exp: Weather is what is happening outside right now — sunny, rainy, hot, cold, windy. It changes daily!

exercises.question: What is CLIMATE?
choices: the average weather pattern of a region over a long period of time
exercises.exp: Climate is the average weather of a place over many years. Canada has a cold climate; the Amazon has a wet tropical climate.

exercises.question: What does a THERMOMETER measure?
exercises.exp: A thermometer measures temperature in degrees Celsius (°C). Water freezes at 0°C and boils at 100°C.

exercises.question: The temperature yesterday was 5°C. Today it is 12°C. What happened to the temperature?
exercises.exp: 12°C − 5°C = 7°C warmer. The temperature rose by 7 degrees.

exercises.question: Which temperature is the WARMEST?
exercises.exp: 15°C is the warmest — it is above zero and higher than the other choices. In Canada that is a nice spring day!

exercises.question: A scientist records the temperature every day for a month. This is called ___.
exercises.exp: Recording measurements over time is collecting data — scientists use this data to find patterns!

exercises.question: Which tool is used to measure RAINFALL?
exercises.exp: A rain gauge is a cylinder that collects rain. Scientists measure how many centimetres fell.

exercises.question: A place that gets very little rain and has hot days and cool nights is ___.
exercises.exp: Deserts have very low rainfall (often less than 25 cm per year) with hot days and cool nights.

exercises.question: What causes SEASONS in Canada?
choices: Earth moving closer to the sun in summer
Earth's tilted axis as it orbits the sun
exercises.exp: Earth's axis is tilted. When Canada tilts toward the sun, we get summer. When tilted away, we get winter.

exercises.question: Which month is likely the COLDEST in Ontario, Canada?
exercises.exp: January is the coldest month in Ontario — temperatures often drop well below 0°C with heavy snowfall.

exercises.question: Scientists make a BAR GRAPH of daily temperatures. What can they learn?
choices: temperature trends and patterns over time
exercises.exp: Bar graphs of temperature data help scientists see trends — like which week was warmest or how temperature changed over time.

exercises.question: When the temperature drops below 0°C, what might happen to rain?
choices: it falls as snow or freezing rain instead
exercises.exp: At 0°C and below, water freezes. Rain can turn to snow, sleet, or freezing rain — winter weather!

exercises.question: What tool measures WIND SPEED?
exercises.exp: An anemometer has cups that spin in the wind — faster spinning = stronger wind. Speed is measured in km/h or m/s.

exercises.question: What tool measures AIR PRESSURE?
exercises.exp: A barometer measures atmospheric pressure. Falling pressure often predicts storms; rising pressure usually means fair weather.

exercises.question: What is a METEOROLOGIST?
choices: a scientist who studies meteors and space rocks
a scientist who studies weather and climate patterns
a scientist who studies rocks and minerals
exercises.exp: Meteorologists study the atmosphere — collecting data from weather stations, satellites, and radar to forecast weather.

exercises.question: CUMULUS clouds are big, puffy, and white. What kind of weather do they usually indicate?
choices: fair, sunny weather — though they can grow into storm clouds if conditions change
exercises.exp: Small cumulus clouds mean fair weather. But when they grow tall (cumulonimbus), they can produce thunderstorms. Learn to read cloud shapes!

exercises.question: STRATUS clouds are flat, grey layers covering the whole sky. What weather do they bring?
choices: overcast skies with possible light rain or drizzle
exercises.exp: Stratus clouds are like a grey blanket covering the sky. They bring dull, overcast conditions and sometimes light drizzle.

exercises.question: A HURRICANE is ___.
choices: a powerful tropical storm with strong spiralling winds around a calm centre (eye)
a cold winter wind from the Arctic
exercises.exp: Hurricanes are massive spinning storm systems forming over warm tropical oceans — with winds over 120 km/h spiralling around a calm 'eye' at the centre.

exercises.question: Forecasters say there is a 70% chance of RAIN tomorrow. What does this mean?
choices: it will definitely rain 70% of the day
based on historical data and current conditions, there is a 70% probability of measurable rain
70% of the city will get rain
exercises.exp: 70% probability means: in similar past conditions, it rained 7 out of 10 times. It might rain, it might not — weather forecasting uses probability!

exercises.question: Why does Canada have FOUR SEASONS?
choices: because Earth moves closer and farther from the sun
because Earth's tilted axis causes different parts to receive more or less direct sunlight as Earth orbits the sun
because Canada is a cold country
exercises.exp: Earth's 23.5° tilt means Canada gets intense, direct summer sun (long days) and weak, low-angle winter sun (short days) — creating seasons as Earth orbits.

exercises.question: Which instrument records weather data AUTOMATICALLY over time?
choices: a datalogger or automatic weather station that records temperature, humidity, and pressure continuously
exercises.exp: Automatic weather stations collect and record data continuously — building long-term records scientists use to find climate patterns and improve forecasts.

exercises.question: What is a TORNADO?
choices: a violently rotating column of air extending from a thunderstorm cloud to the ground
a dust devil in the desert only
exercises.exp: Tornadoes are violently spinning columns of air — the most intense wind storms on Earth, with winds exceeding 400 km/h in extreme cases!

exercises.question: The WATER CYCLE is closely connected to weather because ___.
choices: water only stays in the ocean
evaporation and condensation create clouds and precipitation — driving rain, snow, and storms
water has nothing to do with weather
weather only involves wind, not water
exercises.exp: Weather IS largely the water cycle in action — evaporated ocean water condenses into clouds, falls as rain or snow, and cycles back. Water drives most weather!

exercises.question: OCEAN CURRENTS affect climate because ___.
choices: ocean currents carry warm and cold water around the globe, affecting temperatures of nearby coastal regions
oceans block wind from reaching land
exercises.exp: The Gulf Stream carries warm water to northwest Europe — making it much warmer than other places at the same latitude. Ocean currents are a major climate regulator!

exercises.question: CLIMATE CHANGE is causing global average temperatures to RISE. Which of these is a likely effect?
choices: more frequent and intense extreme weather events, melting ice caps, and rising sea levels
more rainfall in all regions evenly
exercises.exp: Rising temperatures cause: glaciers and polar ice to melt (rising seas), more energy in the atmosphere (stronger storms), changed precipitation patterns, and ecosystem disruption.

exercises.question: A student measures temperature at 8am, 12pm, 4pm, and 8pm every day for a month. This is called ___.
choices: collecting systematic observational data over time
exercises.exp: Systematic, repeated measurement over time is data collection — the foundation of science. Patterns in the data reveal daily and monthly temperature trends.

exercises.question: What is RELATIVE HUMIDITY?
choices: the amount of water vapour in the air compared to the maximum it could hold, expressed as a percentage
the amount of rainfall in a day
exercises.exp: Relative humidity of 100% means the air is holding all the water vapour it can — it is saturated. Humid days feel sticky because sweat evaporates slowly in already-saturated air.

exercises.question: FROST forms when ___.
choices: water vapour deposits directly onto surfaces below 0°C — skipping the liquid stage
exercises.exp: Frost is deposition — water vapour turns directly into ice crystals on cold surfaces (like car windows overnight). No liquid water involved!

exercises.question: Scientists study TREE RINGS and ICE CORES to learn about past climate because ___.
choices: trees and ice are the most accurate thermometers
tree rings record yearly growing conditions and ice cores trap ancient air bubbles — preserving records of past temperature and atmospheric composition
trees and ice only record temperature
ice cores contain living weather records
exercises.exp: Tree rings: wide = good year; narrow = drought/cold. Ice core bubbles contain ancient air — scientists measure CO₂ levels going back 800,000 years. Earth's climate diary!

exercises.question: LAKE-EFFECT SNOW in Ontario happens when cold air passes over warmer Great Lakes water. What causes the heavy snowfall?
choices: the lakes freeze and push snow onto land
cold dry air absorbs moisture and heat from the lake surface, then dumps heavy snow when it hits colder land
the Great Lakes generate wind only
exercises.exp: Cold Arctic air gains heat and moisture from unfrozen lakes. When this now-humid air hits cold land, the moisture dumps as intense, localised snowfall. Cities like Thunder Bay see this!

exercises.question: Why do WEATHER FORECASTS become LESS ACCURATE further into the future?
choices: forecasters do not work on weekends
the atmosphere is a chaotic system — tiny uncertainties in current data grow exponentially over time, making long-range forecasts much less reliable
computers are not powerful enough for 3-day forecasts
weather scientists give up after 24 hours
exercises.exp: The atmosphere is chaotic — small differences in current conditions lead to very different outcomes days later. That is why 10-day forecasts are less reliable than tomorrow's forecast!

exercises.question: The GREENHOUSE EFFECT is ___.
choices: plants in greenhouses making weather change
how greenhouse gases in the atmosphere trap heat from the sun, warming Earth's surface
the process of making oxygen in greenhouses
exercises.exp: Greenhouse gases (CO₂, water vapour, methane) absorb outgoing infrared radiation and re-emit it back to Earth's surface — keeping the planet warm enough for life. Too much = too warm!

exercises.question: What is the difference between WEATHER and CLIMATE?
choices: they are exactly the same thing
weather is the current short-term atmospheric conditions; climate is the average weather pattern of a region over 30+ years
climate is what happens today; weather is the long-term average
exercises.exp: Weather = what is happening NOW (today's rain/sun/temperature). Climate = long-term average patterns. 'Climate is what you expect; weather is what you get!'

exercises.question: Which instrument measures ATMOSPHERIC PRESSURE?
exercises.exp: A barometer measures air pressure. High pressure = usually fair weather. Low pressure = often stormy weather. Barometric changes help predict weather!

exercises.question: An ANEMOMETER measures ___.
exercises.exp: An anemometer measures wind speed — spinning cups catch wind, the faster they spin, the stronger the wind. Essential weather station equipment!

exercises.question: A RAIN GAUGE measures ___.
choices: the amount of rainfall in millimetres over a given period
exercises.exp: A rain gauge collects rainfall in a calibrated tube — read in millimetres. Comparing readings across stations shows precipitation patterns and helps predict floods!

exercises.question: RELATIVE HUMIDITY is ___.
choices: the actual amount of water in air
the percentage of water vapour in air relative to the maximum it could hold at that temperature
the amount of rainfall per day
the temperature at which air becomes saturated
exercises.exp: Relative humidity (RH): 100% = air is saturated (fully loaded with vapour). 50% = air holds half its maximum capacity. High humidity = feels muggy!

exercises.question: The DEW POINT is ___.
choices: the temperature at which water boils
the temperature at which air must be cooled for water vapour to condense (relative humidity reaches 100%)
the point where air pressure is lowest
exercises.exp: Cool air to its dew point and water vapour condenses — forming dew, fog, or clouds. High dew point = humid conditions; low dew point = dry conditions.

exercises.question: A WEATHER FRONT is ___.
choices: the front page of a weather report
the boundary between two air masses of different temperature and/or humidity — often where storms develop
the strongest wind in a storm
exercises.exp: Fronts: where cold and warm air masses meet. Cold fronts bring rapid storms; warm fronts bring gradual cloud and rain. Fronts drive much of our weather!

exercises.question: HURRICANES (tropical cyclones) form over ___.
choices: warm tropical oceans (above 26°C) — warm water provides the heat energy that drives them
exercises.exp: Warm ocean water (26°C+) evaporates rapidly → rising moist air → condensation releases heat → drives the storm system. Hurricanes lose power over land or cold water!

exercises.question: Why are TORNADOES most common in the central USA ('Tornado Alley')?
choices: cold dry Arctic air from Canada meets warm moist Gulf air — creating the unstable conditions perfect for tornado-producing supercell thunderstorms
mountains in surrounding areas direct wind patterns
exercises.exp: Tornado Alley: cold dry air from the north meets warm moist air from the Gulf of Mexico — ideal conditions for the wind shear and instability needed for severe thunderstorms and tornadoes!

exercises.question: CLIMATE ZONES are determined mainly by ___.
choices: the colour of the rock underneath
latitude (distance from equator), altitude, proximity to oceans, and ocean currents
the number of cities in a region
how many rivers cross the area
exercises.exp: Climate depends primarily on latitude (sunlight angle/intensity), but altitude (higher = colder), ocean proximity (moderate temperatures), and currents all significantly modify local climate.

exercises.question: The CORIOLIS EFFECT causes wind and ocean current patterns to ___.
choices: curve to the right in the Northern Hemisphere and to the left in the Southern Hemisphere — due to Earth's rotation
exercises.exp: Earth's rotation causes moving air/water to curve (right in N hemisphere, left in S hemisphere). This creates the spiral of hurricanes and drives global wind patterns!

exercises.question: EL NIÑO is ___.
choices: a periodic warming of surface water in the central and eastern tropical Pacific Ocean — disrupting global weather patterns
a cold ocean current near Antarctica
a monsoon pattern in South Asia
exercises.exp: El Niño: every few years, Pacific trade winds weaken → warm water moves east → affects global weather, causing droughts in Australia, floods in South America, and unusual temperatures worldwide.

exercises.question: The POLAR VORTEX is ___.
choices: a type of hurricane at the North Pole
a large area of low pressure and cold air surrounding Earth's poles — when it weakens, cold Arctic air spills south causing extreme winter weather
a type of permanent cloud formation
exercises.exp: The polar vortex normally keeps frigid Arctic air contained near the poles. When it weakens, cold air escapes southward — causing sudden extreme cold snaps in mid-latitudes!

exercises.question: What causes SEASONS on Earth?
choices: Earth's distance from the sun varying throughout the year
Earth's axial tilt (23.5°) — as Earth orbits the sun, different hemispheres receive more direct sunlight at different times of year
different parts of Earth rotating at different speeds
exercises.exp: Seasons are caused by Earth's 23.5° tilt. When the Northern Hemisphere tilts TOWARD the sun, it receives more direct sunlight and energy = summer. Tilted AWAY = winter!

exercises.question: Which has more DIRECT sunlight (more energy per unit area) and is WARMER?
choices: regions near the poles where sunlight hits at a low angle
regions near the equator where sunlight hits nearly vertically (most concentrated)
regions in the middle latitudes always
all regions receive the same amount of sunlight
exercises.exp: Direct sunlight concentrates energy in a small area — more heat. Low-angle sunlight spreads the same energy over a larger area — less heat. That is why tropics are warm and poles are cold!

exercises.question: OCEAN CURRENTS affect climate because ___.
choices: they distribute heat around the globe — warm currents (like the Gulf Stream) warm coastal climates; cold currents cool them
they have no effect on air above them
they only matter near the equator
exercises.exp: The Gulf Stream carries warm tropical water to Northern Europe — giving London milder winters than equivalent latitudes in Canada. Ocean currents are the planet's heating/cooling system!

exercises.question: Global WARMING refers to ___.
choices: the long-term rise in Earth's average temperature due to increased greenhouse gas concentrations from human activities
warming confined to the poles only
exercises.exp: Global warming: human burning of fossil fuels adds CO₂ to atmosphere → enhanced greenhouse effect → rising global average temperature → climate change effects worldwide.

exercises.question: Which type of cloud is HIGH, THIN, and WISPY (looks like streaks)?
choices: cirrus (high, thin ice crystals, often precede storms)
exercises.exp: Cirrus clouds are high (above 6km), thin, and made of ice crystals. They often indicate an approaching warm front and possible rain in 1-2 days!

exercises.question: ACID RAIN is caused by ___.
choices: only carbon dioxide dissolving in rain
sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxides (from burning fossil fuels) dissolving in rainwater to form sulfuric and nitric acids
temperature inversions trapping acid in valleys
exercises.exp: Acid rain: SO₂ + NOx (from power plants, cars) dissolve in water vapour → sulfuric and nitric acids → pH of rain drops below 5.6 → damages trees, lakes, and stone buildings!
